nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

questions.q: An architect is designing a highly available deployment on OCI and must place resources correctly across the provider's physical hierarchy. How does OCI's physical hierarchy of regions, availability domains (ADs), and fault domains (FDs) work?
choices: A region equals an AD; fault domains are logical groupings of multiple regions
A region always contains exactly three ADs; each AD contains a single fault domain
A region contains a single AD; fault domains span across ADs for redundancy
A region contains one or more ADs; each AD is divided into three fault domains
questions.explanation: An OCI region contains one or more availability domains (each AD is an isolated data centre). Inside every AD there are three fault domains, which are independent groupings of hardware that act as failure isolation zones within the AD. Some newer regions are single-AD, while many commercial regions have three ADs.

questions.q: A finance team needs strict isolation of their OCI resources from engineering, but both groups must roll up to the tenancy's overall cost dashboard. Which OCI construct best fits?
choices: Separate OCI tenancies for finance and engineering
Separate VCNs with no peering between them
Separate compartments under the same tenancy
Separate availability domains for each team
questions.explanation: Compartments are logical containers used to organise, isolate, and control access to resources within a single tenancy; policies on compartments enforce isolation while billing still aggregates at the tenancy level. Separate tenancies would split billing entirely, VCNs only isolate networking (not other resources), and ADs are physical infrastructure rather than an organisational boundary.

questions.q: Which statement is valid OCI IAM policy syntax to let members of the group NetAdmins manage Virtual Cloud Networks in the compartment Network?
choices: allow user NetAdmins to manage virtual-network-family in compartment Network
grant group NetAdmins all on virtual-network-family in compartment Network
permit group NetAdmins manage vcn in compartment Network
allow group NetAdmins to manage virtual-network-family in compartment Network
questions.explanation: OCI policy syntax is: Allow <subject> to <verb> <resource-type> in <location> [where <conditions>]. The subject is normally a group or dynamic group, the verb is inspect/read/use/manage, and virtual-network-family is the aggregate resource type covering VCNs, subnets, gateways, and route tables. Allowing 'user' directly is rare, and 'permit'/'grant' are not valid OCI keywords.

questions.q: You are designing a VCN whose workload must span multiple availability domains for high availability. What is the simplest subnet design?
choices: Create one AD-specific subnet per AD and manually replicate resources
Create regional subnets, which span all availability domains in the region
Create one subnet per fault domain across the region
Use a single AD-specific subnet and rely on cross-region replication
questions.explanation: Regional subnets stretch across every AD in a region, so the same CIDR can host resources in any AD and multi-AD HA designs need only one subnet per tier. AD-specific subnets are a legacy option that force multiple subnets and more IP planning, fault domains do not have their own subnets, and cross-region replication addresses disaster recovery rather than in-region HA.

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

nodes.title: Cloud billing and cost: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud cost optimization is mostly visibility + commitments. You can't optimize what you can't see, and you can't commit without forecasts. Most exams test the savings instruments (reserved instances, savings plans, sustained use) and the visibility tools.

flashcards.front: Where do you see cloud spend?
flashcards.back: AWS Cost Explorer / Azure Cost Management / GCP Billing reports. Filter by tag, service, account, region. Set up budget alerts (notify when 80% / 100% of monthly budget is hit) so a runaway autoscaler doesn't surprise you on the 28th.

flashcards.front: Reserved Instance vs Savings Plan vs Spot — pick the right one.
flashcards.back: RI / committed-use: 1-3 yr commitment, 30-60% off, locked to instance family/region. Savings Plan: 1-3 yr commitment on $/hr spend, more flexible across instance types. Spot/preemptible: up to 90% off, can be reclaimed any moment. Use commitments for steady baseline, spot for fault-tolerant workloads.

flashcards.front: What's the egress (data transfer out) cost trap?
flashcards.back: Most clouds charge nothing to ingest data but $0.05-$0.12/GB to send it OUT. Inter-region replication, public-facing APIs, multi-cloud data movement — all add up fast. Mitigations: same-region peering, CloudFront / CDN caching, VPC endpoints to keep traffic on the AWS backbone.

flashcards.front: What is a unit cost / cost per X?
flashcards.back: Cost-per-request, cost-per-active-user, cost-per-transaction. Total cloud spend is a vanity metric — engineers can't act on '$50k/month'. Unit cost ($0.003 per request) reveals whether you got cheaper or more expensive as you scaled, which is what optimization actually means.

questions.q: A team is choosing between Oracle Autonomous Database and a self-managed OCI Database System and wants to know what they gain that the self-managed option cannot match. Which capability is unique to Oracle Autonomous Database compared with a self-managed OCI Database System?
choices: Automated patching, backups, scaling, and tuning fully managed by Oracle
Support for the SQL language and PL/SQL
Multi-AD high availability via Data Guard
Pay-per-use OCPU-hour billing
questions.explanation: Autonomous Database is a self-driving managed database whose distinguishing feature is automation of patching, backups, scaling, and performance tuning by Oracle. SQL and PL/SQL are supported by both Autonomous and self-managed Database Systems, multi-AD Data Guard configurations are available on both, and pay-per-use billing applies to both as well.

questions.q: A student wants to run a small Autonomous Database and a Compute instance indefinitely on OCI without being billed. Which description of Always Free resources is correct?
choices: They are only usable during the 30-day Free Trial period and disabled afterwards
They are available indefinitely at no cost within published limits, even after the trial ends
They require a paid subscription but include 300 US dollars in monthly credits
They are only available in OCI Government Cloud regions
questions.explanation: OCI's Always Free programme provides resources such as two AMD VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro instances, two Autonomous Databases, 200 GB of Block Volume, and 20 GB of Object Storage that remain free indefinitely within published quotas, even after the 30-day Free Trial expires. The separate Free Trial provides a one-time US$300 credit usable against paid services and lasts 30 days; both make up the OCI Free Tier.

questions.q: Which OCI service should be used to centrally generate, store, and rotate encryption keys and secrets such as database passwords?
choices: OCI Vault
OCI Bastion
OCI Identity Domains
OCI Audit
questions.explanation: OCI Vault is a managed service that creates and manages master encryption keys (optionally HSM-backed) and stores secrets like passwords or API tokens with versioning and rotation. OCI Bastion brokers secure SSH or RDP sessions into private resources, Identity Domains is the IAM identity layer for users and federation, and Audit captures API activity logs for compliance.

questions.q: A customer commits to a one-year spend with Oracle in exchange for discounted rates and the freedom to consume any OCI service against that committed amount. Which pricing model is this?
choices: Pay As You Go (PAYG)
Annual Universal Credits
Bring Your Own License (BYOL)
Government Cloud pricing
questions.explanation: Annual Universal Credits represent a committed annual spend that can be applied to any OCI service at discounted rates compared with PAYG. PAYG is on-demand consumption with no commitment, BYOL lets customers re-use existing on-premises Oracle licences to lower OCI database or middleware costs, and Government Cloud pricing applies to a separate region offering for US government workloads.
